title: General Biochemistry II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L General Biochemistry II curriculum, continuing from BCH201: bioenergetics and thermodynamics, high-energy compounds, biological oxidation and the electron transport chain/oxidative phosphorylation, introductory enzyme concepts, vitamins and coenzymes, nucleotide/nucleic acid structure, and acid-base/buffer physiology (haemoglobin, blood pH). Detailed enzyme kinetics is left to BCH301 and detailed pathway metabolism to the 300L metabolism courses.

questions.question: In biochemical thermodynamics, a reaction with a negative standard free energy change (ΔG°') is described as:
questions.explanation: A negative ΔG°' means the reaction releases free energy and proceeds spontaneously under standard conditions, which defines an exergonic reaction.

questions.question: Why is ATP referred to as a 'high-energy' compound?
options: Hydrolysis of its phosphoanhydride bonds releases a large amount of free energy due to charge repulsion relief and resonance stabilisation of products
It contains a large number of carbon-carbon double bonds
It is synthesised only inside the cell nucleus
Its molecular weight is higher than that of most other cellular molecules
questions.correct_answer: Hydrolysis of its phosphoanhydride bonds releases a large amount of free energy due to charge repulsion relief and resonance stabilisation of products
questions.explanation: The phosphoanhydride bonds in ATP are 'high-energy' because hydrolysis relieves electrostatic repulsion between adjacent negatively charged phosphates and the products are stabilised by resonance, giving a large negative ΔG.

questions.question: Two reactions can be 'coupled' in metabolism when:
options: An exergonic reaction drives an endergonic reaction because they share a common intermediate
They occur in different cells of the same organism
They are catalysed by enzymes with the same EC number
questions.correct_answer: An exergonic reaction drives an endergonic reaction because they share a common intermediate
questions.explanation: Energy coupling links an energetically favourable reaction to an unfavourable one via a shared intermediate (often ATP/ADP), allowing the overall combined reaction to proceed.

questions.question: In the electron transport chain, which complex is also known as NADH dehydrogenase and is the entry point for electrons from NADH?
questions.explanation: Complex I (NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase) accepts electrons from NADH and passes them to ubiquinone, pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane in the process.

questions.question: Which electron transport chain complex is the final electron acceptor site, transferring electrons to molecular oxygen to form water?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) catalyses the final step of the electron transport chain, reducing O2 to H2O using electrons delivered by cytochrome c.

questions.question: The chemiosmotic theory of oxidative phosphorylation, proposed by Peter Mitchell, states that ATP synthesis is driven by:
options: A proton-motive force generated by electron transport chain pumping of H+ across the inner mitochondrial membrane
Direct phosphorylation of ADP by NADH
The diffusion of oxygen into the mitochondrial matrix
questions.correct_answer: A proton-motive force generated by electron transport chain pumping of H+ across the inner mitochondrial membrane
questions.explanation: Chemiosmosis proposes that electron transport pumps protons into the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical gradient whose energy drives ATP synthase to make ATP as protons flow back into the matrix.

questions.question: Which compound is the mobile electron carrier that shuttles electrons between Complex III and Complex IV in the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c is a small, water-soluble haem protein loosely associated with the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane that carries electrons from Complex III to Complex IV.

questions.question: A cofactor is best defined as:
options: A non-protein chemical component required by an enzyme for catalytic activity
The substrate that an enzyme acts upon
The product released after an enzyme-catalysed reaction
A protein that inhibits enzyme activity irreversibly
questions.correct_answer: A non-protein chemical component required by an enzyme for catalytic activity
questions.explanation: Cofactors are non-protein helper molecules (metal ions or organic coenzymes) that enzymes need to be catalytically active; the protein portion alone is called the apoenzyme.

questions.question: An enzyme's complete, catalytically active complex of apoenzyme plus its cofactor is called the:
questions.explanation: Holoenzyme refers to the fully functional enzyme, i.e. the protein (apoenzyme) bound to its required cofactor/coenzyme.

questions.question: Which vitamin is the precursor for the coenzymes NAD+ and NADP+?
questions.explanation: Niacin is converted in the body to nicotinamide, which forms part of the NAD+/NADP+ coenzymes central to redox reactions.

questions.question: Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), derived from vitamin B1, serves as an essential coenzyme for which type of reaction?
options: Decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids, such as in the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction
Transfer of one-carbon units in nucleotide synthesis
Hydroxylation of proline in collagen synthesis
questions.correct_answer: Decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids, such as in the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction
questions.explanation: TPP is the coenzyme for enzymes that decarboxylate alpha-keto acids, including pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

questions.question: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is the precursor of which two coenzymes?
questions.explanation: Riboflavin is converted into flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), both flavin coenzymes used in redox reactions.

questions.question: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a structural component of which important metabolic cofactor?
questions.explanation: Pantothenic acid is incorporated into coenzyme A, which activates acyl groups (e.g. acetyl-CoA) for transfer in metabolism.

questions.question: A deficiency of vitamin B1 (thiamine) causes which classical disease?
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency impairs carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function, classically producing beriberi (wet or dry forms).

questions.question: Deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3) classically causes which disease, characterised by dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia?
questions.explanation: Pellagra results from niacin (or tryptophan) deficiency and is classically described by the '3 Ds': dermatitis, diarrhoea, and dementia.

questions.question: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential cofactor for enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine during the synthesis of which protein?
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid is required by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases for collagen maturation; its deficiency causes scurvy due to defective collagen cross-linking.

questions.question: Which vitamin functions as a coenzyme in transamination and decarboxylation reactions of amino acid metabolism?
questions.explanation: Pyridoxal phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, is a coenzyme for transaminases and decarboxylases involved in amino acid metabolism.

questions.question: Biotin functions biochemically as a coenzyme for which class of enzymes?
questions.explanation: Biotin is covalently attached to carboxylase enzymes and acts as a mobile carrier of CO2 in carboxylation reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase.

questions.question: A pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base, and one or more phosphate groups combine to form the basic structural unit of nucleic acids known as a:
questions.explanation: A nucleotide consists of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base, and phosphate group(s); a nucleoside lacks the phosphate.

questions.question: Which pair correctly lists the purine bases found in nucleic acids?
questions.explanation: Adenine and guanine are double-ringed purine bases; cytosine, thymine and uracil are single-ringed pyrimidines.

questions.question: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs specifically with thymine via how many hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine via how many?
questions.explanation: Chargaff/Watson-Crick base pairing specifies two hydrogen bonds between adenine and thymine and three between guanine and cytosine, giving G-C pairs greater thermal stability.

questions.question: The sugar found in RNA differs from that in DNA in that RNA's ribose has:
options: A hydroxyl (-OH) group at the 2' carbon, whereas DNA's deoxyribose has only hydrogen there
An extra phosphate group at the 5' carbon
A nitrogenous base attached at the 1' carbon that DNA lacks
questions.correct_answer: A hydroxyl (-OH) group at the 2' carbon, whereas DNA's deoxyribose has only hydrogen there
questions.explanation: Ribose (in RNA) has a 2'-OH group; deoxyribose (in DNA) lacks oxygen at the 2' position, hence the name 'deoxy'.

questions.question: According to Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA, which relationship holds true?
options: The amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and guanine equals cytosine
The amount of purines always equals the amount of pyrimidines in any single-stranded nucleic acid
Adenine equals guanine in all organisms
The total base content is identical across all species
questions.correct_answer: The amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine, and guanine equals cytosine
questions.explanation: Chargaff's rule (A=T, G=C) reflects the complementary base pairing in double-stranded DNA, later explained structurally by Watson and Crick.

questions.question: Haemoglobin's ability to bind oxygen cooperatively -- where binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity for subsequent O2 molecules -- is best explained by which model?
options: A conformational shift from the low-affinity 'tense' (T) state to the high-affinity 'relaxed' (R) state
Irreversible covalent modification of the haem iron
Simple mass-action binding with no interaction between subunits
Complete replacement of Fe2+ with Fe3+ upon oxygen binding
questions.correct_answer: A conformational shift from the low-affinity 'tense' (T) state to the high-affinity 'relaxed' (R) state
questions.explanation: Haemoglobin's cooperativity arises because oxygen binding at one subunit favours the transition of the tetramer from the low-affinity T state to the high-affinity R state, increasing affinity at the remaining subunits.

questions.question: The Bohr effect describes how haemoglobin's oxygen affinity is:
options: Decreased by a fall in pH (rise in H+) and by increased CO2, promoting O2 release in metabolically active tissue
Increased by a fall in pH, promoting greater O2 uptake in tissues
Unaffected by pH or CO2 concentration
Decreased only by temperature changes, never by pH
questions.correct_answer: Decreased by a fall in pH (rise in H+) and by increased CO2, promoting O2 release in metabolically active tissue
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect describes the physiological adaptation whereby increased H+ and CO2 (as in actively respiring tissue) lower haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, favouring O2 unloading where it is needed most.

questions.question: Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, when the concentration of a buffer's conjugate base equals the concentration of its weak acid, the solution's pH equals:
options: The pKa of the weak acid
questions.correct_answer: The pKa of the weak acid
questions.explanation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); when [A-] = [HA], the log term is log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa.

questions.question: The bicarbonate buffer system (H2CO3/HCO3-) is the principal extracellular buffer in blood mainly because:
options: It is an open system in which CO2 can be rapidly eliminated or retained by the lungs, allowing tight regulation of blood pH
Bicarbonate has the lowest solubility of all blood buffers
It has a pKa that is much lower than physiological blood pH
It does not involve the respiratory system at all
questions.correct_answer: It is an open system in which CO2 can be rapidly eliminated or retained by the lungs, allowing tight regulation of blood pH
questions.explanation: Because CO2 can be exhaled or retained via ventilation, the bicarbonate buffer system is an 'open' system that the body can adjust dynamically, making it physiologically powerful despite a pKa (~6.1) below blood pH (7.4).

questions.question: A blood pH below 7.35 due to a primary decrease in plasma bicarbonate is classified as:
questions.explanation: Metabolic acidosis results from a primary fall in HCO3- (e.g. from diarrhoea, ketoacidosis, or renal failure) lowering blood pH below normal.

questions.question: Prolonged hyperventilation, which excessively blows off CO2, tends to cause which acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation reduces plasma CO2 (and therefore carbonic acid), raising blood pH above normal, i.e. respiratory alkalosis.

questions.question: Which statement about enzyme active sites is correct?
options: The active site is a three-dimensional cleft or pocket, often formed from amino acid residues that are distant in the primary sequence but brought together by folding
The active site is identical in chemical composition to the substrate
Every amino acid in an enzyme directly participates in catalysis at the active site
The active site is always located at the enzyme's N-terminus
questions.correct_answer: The active site is a three-dimensional cleft or pocket, often formed from amino acid residues that are distant in the primary sequence but brought together by folding
questions.explanation: Protein folding brings together specific residues from different parts of the polypeptide chain to form the catalytically active three-dimensional active site.

questions.question: The 'induced fit' model of enzyme-substrate binding proposes that:
options: The enzyme's active site changes shape slightly upon substrate binding to achieve an optimal fit for catalysis
Substrates are rigid and enzymes are perfectly rigid complementary locks
Only competitive inhibitors can induce a conformational change in enzymes
Substrate binding never alters enzyme conformation
questions.correct_answer: The enzyme's active site changes shape slightly upon substrate binding to achieve an optimal fit for catalysis
questions.explanation: Koshland's induced-fit model proposes that substrate binding induces a conformational adjustment in the enzyme that improves the geometric and chemical fit for catalysis, unlike the earlier rigid lock-and-key idea.

questions.question: The standard free energy change for ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi) under cellular conditions is approximately:
questions.explanation: The standard free energy of ATP hydrolysis is commonly cited as approximately -30.5 kJ/mol (about -7.3 kcal/mol), reflecting its role as a high-energy phosphate carrier.

questions.question: Substrate-level phosphorylation differs from oxidative phosphorylation in that it:
options: Generates ATP directly from a high-energy phosphorylated metabolic intermediate, without involvement of the electron transport chain
Only occurs in the presence of oxygen
Requires the proton-motive force across the mitochondrial membrane
Is catalysed exclusively by ATP synthase
questions.correct_answer: Generates ATP directly from a high-energy phosphorylated metabolic intermediate, without involvement of the electron transport chain
questions.explanation: Substrate-level phosphorylation transfers a phosphate group directly from a high-energy intermediate (e.g. 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate, phosphoenolpyruvate) to ADP, independent of the electron transport chain, and can occur even without oxygen.
